Summary:

In their manuscript, Pathak/Gueguinou et al. investigate the role of the mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, NCLX, in colorectal cancer (CRC) cell proliferation and invasion. The primary experimental models used to address these questions include colon cancer cell lines (HCT226, DLD1) in which NCLX was constitutively knocked out (CRISPR/Cas9) or transiently knocked down (siRNA), as well as NCLX-/- mice in which NCLX was knocked out globally using the CRISPR/Cas9 system. The authors found that NCLX expression is downregulated in colorectal tumors from CRC patients, exhibiting a greater decrease in advanced-stage patients, and showed that NLCX knockout in mice resulted in fewer, smaller tumors in a DSS-induced colonic tumor model. NLCX knockout/knockdown in vitro caused mitochondrial Ca2+ (mtCa2+) overload owing to abrogated NLCX-mediated mtCa2+ efflux in the context of largely unchanged MCU-mediated Ca2+ influx into mitochondria and, as a consequence, led to overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS). It also disrupted mitochondrial membranes and cristae, induced expression of mitophagy markers, caused mitochondrial membrane depolarization, and negatively affected respiratory reserve. Notably, they found that NLCX knockout/knockdown suppressed proliferation of CRC cells, but enhanced CRC cell migration; it also increased chemoresistance and expression of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and hypoxia (i.e., hypoxia-inducible factor 1α [HIF1α]), as well as stem cell-related genes. The authors conclude that loss of NCLX expression and accompanying mitochondrial Ca2+ overload drives the metastatic behavior of CRC cells through ROS-dependent activation of HIF1α and altered expression of HIF1α target genes.

Essential revisions:

Overall

Using a broad range of experimental approaches, the authors tell a convincing story about the functional consequences of NCLX downregulation in CRC, showing that, although loss of NCLX suppresses cancer cell proliferation, it also enhances cell migratory behavior. Thus, the NCLX downregulation in CRC exerts a net detrimental effect owing to an associated increase in metastatic potential. The experimental models (wild-type and NCLX-KO/KD CRC cells, wild-type and NCLX-/- mouse DSS-induced colonic tumor models, patient-derived CRC tumors) are complementary and generally appropriate, and the conclusions follow logically from the results. Overall, these findings significantly advance our understanding of the contribution of mitochondrial Ca2+ dynamics to CRC progression and suggest NCLX as a potential therapeutic target.

General comments

A unified approach should be applied to the presentation of results from the various HT116 and DLD1 NCLX-KO clones. In some cases, results from all NCLX-KO clones are shown in figure panels, but in others, results from only a subset (or even just one) clone are presented. Results from all clones should be shown throughout or results from a representative clone (or clones) of each cell type should be consistently shown. Choosing to show results from one clone but not others in some experimental settings leaves the impression of cherry picking.

Awkward phrasing and grammatical errors are frequent enough to significantly impact readability and occasionally obscure meaning. Recommend additional editing efforts.

1) Only circumstantial evidence supports the claim that NCLX expression controls tumor progression via matrix calcium. It has to be shown that MCU deletion prevents the effect of NCLX in colorectal tumor cells in at least in one of the paradigms. The Authors propose that the effect of NCLX targeting on the tumor growth and metastasis formation is mediated through mitochondrial matrix [Ca2+]. However, an alternative possibility is that NCLX per se has a function in the tumors. Studying the MCU-deficient cells would help to discriminate between these distinct possibilities. Losing the tumor growth/metastasis effects of NCLX targeting in MCU-deficient cells would directly support the Authors' proposal, and the opposite result would be conclusive evidence that NCLX is relevant for the tumors independent of matrix calcium signaling.

After discussion, the reviewers felt that conclusion should be rephrased to leave open the possibility that the NCLX effect is not mediated through matrix [Ca2+].

2) Although the results of Figure 2 are very interesting, the reasons that an intrasplenic injection was chosen are not explained. In this model, metastasis to the colon was measured and not the other way around. Some discussion of why this injection site was chosen and of the limitations of this system would be helpful to better appreciate this experiment.

3) In Figure 3—figure supplement 1L, there appears to be a several-fold increase in cleaved caspase 3 positive cells. For some reason, this is reported as a slight increase in apoptosis and then discounted. I don't quite understand the reasons for this conclusion. The average number of cells exhibiting cleaved caspase 3 increases from less than 10% to around 30%. Why can't this be responsible for the decrease in total cell number over time? Particularly when you consider the growth curves were not logarithmic, which could be explained by apoptosis?

4) Also, in Figure 3, there is a statement that differences in MMP activity are greater than differences in MMP expression. This statement can be easily tested statistically; please do so or remove the statement.

5) The basis for the statement that mitophagy is increased in NCLX-KO cells is unclear to me based on the data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2. Evidence is provided that mitochondria are damaged and exhibit less cristae. It is shown that there is more LC3BII, which could indicate the presence of more autophagic vesicles, however, there is also increased P62 expression in Figure 4; P62 is degraded during autophagy. There is also no loss of total mitochondria as shown in Figure 4D. As such, while these data definitely show mitochondrial damage, I do not understand the reasons for attributing it to increased mitophagy.

6) In the Discussion section, there is a statement that reduced expression of cell cycle-related genes in NCLX-KO cells is consistent with decreased proliferation. Does this refer to decreased expression of genes associated with the G2/M checkpoint? If so, the data shown isn't entirely sufficient to make this claim; are the genes that are downregulated within the G2/M checkpoint category all genes that promote proliferation?

7) Figure 3—figure supplement 1L: Was the increase in cleaved caspase-3 detected in all three HT116 clones, or was only clone #33 tested?

8) In the absence of more direct approaches for assessing apoptosis, the suggestion that apoptosis is generally increased in NCLX-KO CRC cells based on an increase in cleaved caspase-3 (as implied by the text) is an overinterpretation.

9) "Collectively, these results show that the loss of NCLX in CRC cells causes an increase in migration and invasion of CRC cells through increased MMP1, 2, and 9 protein levels and activity." This conclusion should be toned down. No experiments capable of establishing a causal relationship between MMP increases and migration/invasion (MMP KO, MMP inhibitors, etc.) were done. At best, these expression and zymography data are suggestive of the involvement of MMPs.

10) Figure 3: Despite the fact that MMP1 showed the strongest increase in protein expression among the three MMPs tested (Figure 3L,M), zymography results are only shown for MMP2 and MMP9. Why?

11) Loss of NCLX in CRC cells inhibits mtCa2+ extrusion, causes mitochondrial perturbations, and enhances mitophagy and mitochondrial ROS.

12) "While basal and ATP-dependent OCR were slightly decreased…"

No. In the main figure (Figure 4K), basal OCR was significantly decreased whereas ATP-dependent OCR was not. "Slightly decreased" is a vague phrase that cannot be used to simultaneously describe both significant and non-significant differences (any "difference" that does not reach statistical significance should be described as a trend or tendency).

13) Although the different DLD1 clones yielded OCR results that were generally consistent with each other (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), exhibiting significant decreases in basal, spare, ATP-dependent and max OCR, they differed from those of clone #33 HCT116 NCLX-KO cells with respect to ATP-dependent OCR (Figure 4K). Curiously, although results for all HCT116 NCLX-KO clones were presented in Figure 4A,D,E,F,G,H and I, data for HCT116 NCLX-KO clones #37 and #59 were not shown in Figure 4K, making it difficult to gauge the significance of this discrepancy. These additional data should be shown.

14) "non-significant reduction" is an oxymoron: if it isn't significant, it isn't a reduction. Modifying this phrase with "mild" just further confuses the issue.

15) In the seahorse experiments, every parameter seems to be lower in the NCLX-KO (basal, oligomyicin, uncoupled and even after Rotenone/Antimycin), this raises the concern that such a reduction could be caused simply by a lower total number of cells at the moment of the experiment (due to attachment, growth, cell death, etc) or lower number of mitochondria. While the latter is trickier to assess, the former can be done by washing the wells in the seahorse plates with PBS to remove dead/detached cells and then doing protein extraction from the wells with RIPA buffer (and use that to normalize the values rather than the amount of cells plated, which could vary between the groups due to cell attachment, death and growth during the short time they stay in culture in the plates).

16) Why is colorectal cancer chosen to study the effect of NCLX expression? Did the authors have some prior knowledge or some supporting data of the involvement of NCLX in colorectal cancer specifically?

Do the risk factors of colorectal cancer like smoking, alcohol consumption or genetic predisposition have any effect on NCLX expression levels? From the data set available to the authors or the patient samples available (if the patient background history is available), can something be concluded in this respect?

17) NCLX loss (1) inhibits proliferation and primary tumor growth, while (2) enhancing metastasis, and drug resistance, suggesting that a loss of NCLX contributes to CRC metastatic progression. How is the expression of NCLX different (if any) in the metastatic part of the tumor (i.e. at the secondary site of the tumor)?

18) Do all samples obtained from patients with colorectal cancer or the information available in the database have NCLX dowregulation? If no, then what percentage of the available dataset has this NCLX downregulation?

results.result: NCLX (SLC8B1) mRNA expression is significantly downregulated in colorectal cancer tumors compared to normal tissue across multiple patient cohorts and histological subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C7, C8, and C12 collectively demonstrate consistent downregulation of NCLX mRNA in CRC tumors using both TCGA database analysis and independent patient samples from Penn State University Medical Center. The findings are replicated across different age groups and histological subtypes (adenocarcinoma and mucinous adenocarcinoma), providing robust evidence for this result.

results.result: NCLX expression levels in colorectal tumors are independent of patient sex and KRAS/PI3K mutation status.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C4 show no significant differences in SLC8B1 mRNA levels based on sex or KRAS/PI3K mutation status using TCGA data. These negative findings are important for characterizing the pattern of NCLX downregulation in CRC and are supported by appropriate statistical analyses.

results.result: Low NCLX expression is associated with TP53 mutations and wild-type BRAF in colorectal tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C6 demonstrate specific associations between NCLX expression and genetic alterations in CRC. The TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1D supports these associations, though the mechanistic basis for these relationships remains unexplored.

results.result: NCLX expression progressively decreases with advancing tumor stage, with significantly lower levels in late-stage (III/IV) compared to early-stage (I/II) colorectal cancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C10, C11, and C13 demonstrate a clear correlation between NCLX loss and disease progression. This is supported by both TCGA database analysis and independent patient samples from Penn State, showing consistent stage-dependent reduction in NCLX expression across multiple datasets.

results.result: NCLX knockout mice develop approximately 50% fewer and smaller tumors with reduced dysplasia in the AOM-DSS colitis-associated colorectal cancer model.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C15, and C16 provide consistent in vivo evidence that NCLX loss reduces primary tumor burden. The data from tumor counts, size measurements, and histological analyses (Figures 1I-M) with n≥30 mice per group provide robust statistical support for this finding.

results.result: Loss of NCLX in HCT116 cells reduces primary tumor growth in xenograft models as measured by bioluminescence and tumor volume.
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C18, and C19 demonstrate reduced primary tumor growth in NCLX KO xenografts using multiple independent measurements (bioluminescence flux and physical tumor volume). The data from 15 mice per group with longitudinal imaging provides strong evidence for this anti-proliferative effect.

results.result: Despite reduced primary tumor growth, NCLX knockout dramatically increases metastasis to liver and colon, reduces overall survival, and is the primary cause of lethality in xenograft models.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C24 establish the dichotomous role of NCLX loss: reduced primary tumor growth but increased metastasis and mortality. The bioluminescence imaging, tissue analysis, and survival data (Figure 2) provide compelling evidence for this paradoxical phenotype, which is the central finding of the manuscript.

results.result: NCLX loss reduces CRC cell proliferation and increases apoptosis, likely explaining the reduced tumor size observed in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 provide mechanistic insight into reduced tumor growth through proliferation assays (CyQUANT) and apoptosis markers (cleaved caspase-3). The consistency across multiple NCLX KO clones and knockdown approaches strengthens this conclusion, though the apoptosis data relies primarily on a single marker.

results.result: NCLX loss significantly increases CRC cell migration in gap closure assays, independent of proliferation effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 demonstrate increased migration across multiple NCLX KO clones and knockdown conditions. The use of early time points (6 hr) and mitomycin C treatment effectively rules out proliferation as a confounding factor, providing strong evidence for a genuine pro-migratory effect.

results.result: NCLX loss increases CRC cell invasion through upregulation of matrix metalloproteinases (MMP1, MMP2, MMP9) at the mRNA, protein, and activity levels, with post-transcriptional regulation playing a major role.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 provide comprehensive evidence for increased invasive capacity through Matrigel invasion assays, RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and zymography. The observation that MMP activity increases more than mRNA/protein levels (C37) suggests post-transcriptional regulation, though this inference could benefit from additional mechanistic studies.

results.result: NCLX loss reduces mitochondrial Ca2+ extrusion without affecting uptake, leading to mitochondrial Ca2+ overload and decreased cytosolic Ca2+ entry.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 establish the primary biochemical consequence of NCLX loss using Rhod-2 AM and Fura-2 calcium imaging across multiple cell lines and experimental approaches (KO and siRNA). The consistency with previous work (C41) and the comprehensive calcium measurements provide strong support for this fundamental mechanism.

results.result: NCLX loss causes mitochondrial depolarization and structural abnormalities including disrupted cristae in 60-70% of mitochondria, without changing overall mitochondrial area.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 demonstrate mitochondrial dysfunction through TMRE flow cytometry and detailed TEM analysis. The quantitative TEM data showing specific cristae disruption without area changes provides strong morphological evidence, though the mechanism linking Ca2+ overload to cristae disruption requires further investigation.

results.result: NCLX loss increases autophagosome formation as evidenced by elevated LC3BII and p62 protein levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 show increased LC3BII and p62 levels, but the simultaneous increase in both markers is problematic. Since p62 is typically degraded during autophagy, the concurrent elevation suggests either autophagosome accumulation without completion of autophagy or impaired autophagic flux. Additional experiments (e.g., autophagy flux assays) are needed to clarify whether this represents increased autophagy initiation or blockade.

results.result: NCLX loss significantly reduces maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity in CRC cells without affecting expression of respiratory complex components, with cell line-specific effects on basal respiration.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 demonstrate impaired mitochondrial respiratory capacity using Seahorse OCR measurements. The finding that respiratory complex protein levels are unchanged (C57) suggests functional rather than expression-level defects. The cell line-specific differences in basal respiration (reduced in DLD1 but not HCT116) indicate context-dependent effects that warrant further investigation.

results.result: NCLX loss increases mitochondrial ROS production as measured by MitoSOX in multiple CRC cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 demonstrate increased mtROS across multiple NCLX KO clones and knockdown conditions in three different CRC cell lines using both flow cytometry and fluorescence microscopy. The consistency across experimental approaches and cell lines provides robust evidence for this key mechanistic link.

results.result: NCLX knockout drives transcriptional reprogramming toward pro-metastatic pathways (hypoxia, EMT, glycolysis, inflammation) while suppressing proliferative pathways (Myc targets, cell cycle, OXPHOS), resembling the mesenchymal CMS4 CRC subtype.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 provide comprehensive transcriptomic evidence through RNA-seq and GSEA analysis. The gene expression signatures mirror the observed phenotypes (reduced proliferation, increased metastasis) and align with the aggressive CMS4 subtype. However, the comparison to CMS4 (C65) is correlative and would benefit from direct validation in CMS4 patient samples.

results.result: NCLX loss upregulates stem cell markers (NANOG, Oct4, Sox2, Foxo3) and glutathione synthesis pathway regulators (SLC7A11, GCLM), conferring stem cell-like properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 demonstrate increased expression of stem cell markers by RT-qPCR across multiple NCLX KO clones. The connection to glutathione synthesis is supported by citation to prior work in breast cancer. However, functional validation of stem cell properties (e.g., sphere formation, limiting dilution assays) would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: NCLX loss confers resistance to 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) chemotherapy, with NCLX KO cells showing higher IC50 values and maintained proliferation and migration despite 5-FU treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 demonstrate chemoresistance through IC50 measurements and functional assays. The nearly 2-fold increase in IC50 (8.2 to 15 μM) and preserved migration in NCLX KO cells provide strong evidence for 5-FU resistance, which has important clinical implications for CRC treatment.

results.result: NCLX loss stabilizes HIF1α protein through an mtROS-dependent mechanism independent of mTORC1 signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C79 establish HIF1α as a key mediator of NCLX loss phenotypes. The rescue of HIF1α stabilization by mitoTEMPO (C76) provides strong evidence for mtROS-dependent regulation. The exclusion of mTORC1 involvement through S6K1 phosphorylation analysis (C77-C78) strengthens the mechanistic model, though other potential regulatory pathways remain unexplored.

results.result: The mitochondrial antioxidant mitoTEMPO reduces migration of NCLX KO cells without affecting proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C80 and C81 demonstrate that mtROS specifically drives the migratory phenotype but not the proliferative defect in NCLX KO cells. This selective rescue experiment provides important mechanistic insight into the dichotomous roles of NCLX loss, though the lack of effect on proliferation suggests additional ROS-independent mechanisms.

results.result: NCLX loss upregulates glycolytic genes (GLUT1, HK2, ALDOA, ENO1, LDHA) at mRNA and protein levels while downregulating pentose phosphate pathway genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 demonstrate a metabolic shift toward glycolysis through RT-qPCR and Western blotting across multiple NCLX KO clones and knockdown conditions. The concurrent downregulation of pentose phosphate pathway genes (C85) suggests a specific metabolic reprogramming, though the functional consequences of this pathway suppression require further investigation.

results.result: NCLX loss increases glycolytic flux as measured by ECAR, glucose dependency, glucose consumption, and lactate production, compensating for reduced respiratory capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 provide functional validation of the glycolytic shift through Seahorse ECAR measurements and direct metabolite quantification. The interpretation that this compensates for reduced respiratory capacity (C88) is reasonable given the OCR data, representing a classic Warburg-like metabolic adaptation.

results.result: Glycolysis inhibition with 2-DG abrogates the enhanced migration of NCLX KO cells, suggesting glycolysis supports migration and represents a potential therapeutic target.
results.evaluation: Claims C89 and C90 demonstrate that glycolysis is functionally required for the enhanced migration phenotype through 2-DG rescue experiments. However, C91's suggestion of therapeutic targeting is speculative and would require extensive additional validation including in vivo efficacy studies and assessment of normal tissue toxicity.

results.result: Background on mitochondrial calcium homeostasis, NCLX function, and the role of mitochondrial calcium in cancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C109 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the scientific context for the study, including the roles of mitochondria in cancer (C92-C94), mitochondrial calcium signaling (C95-C102), altered mtCa2+ in cancer (C103-C105), and the specific importance of NCLX (C106-C109). All claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Background on colorectal cancer epidemiology, clinical significance, and molecular classification systems (CMS and CRIS).
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C115 provide relevant background on CRC incidence, mortality, and molecular classification. These claims establish the clinical context and importance of the study, particularly the relevance of the CMS4 mesenchymal subtype (C114) to the observed NCLX loss phenotype. All claims are appropriately cited.

results.result: Loss of NCLX is a novel driver of metastasis, and regulation of mtCa2+ represents a novel therapeutic approach in metastatic colorectal cancer.
results.evaluation: Claim C116 is supported by the extensive experimental evidence showing increased metastasis in NCLX loss models. However, C117's assertion that mtCa2+ regulation is a therapeutic approach is highly speculative. The study demonstrates that NCLX loss promotes metastasis, but therapeutic restoration of NCLX or modulation of mtCa2+ would require extensive additional studies including druggability assessment, efficacy testing, and safety evaluation.
